text: This project is about live research agents whose results get verified. Every week, new forecasting models are published with claims about how good they are. Our agents find those claims, check them against their sources, and then measure them on our own data. We picked electricity load as the test case. It is a hot topic for two reasons: energy demand is growing, in part because of data centers, and foundation models for time series have improved quickly. A disclaimer: week-ahead load forecasting is a well-known problem. We are not trying to beat what power providers and energy hedge funds already model. We chose it because these forecasts run fast enough to build and test the whole idea in a hackathon, and because they show weather doing real work as an input.

Power cannot be stored cheaply, so grid operators schedule power plants from a forecast of demand, called load. PJM is the largest grid operator in the United States. A few percent of forecast error is real money, so every new forecasting model gets attention.

Our test bed is hourly load in four PJM zones. We started with Jersey Central in New Jersey and Dominion in Virginia. Then we kept two more zones back for a fresh test: AEP, which stretches from Indiana to Virginia, and Atlantic City Electric in southern New Jersey.
Every Monday at midnight, each method forecasts the next 168 hours. Here is one week: the actual load, a plain regression, and Chronos-2, a pretrained model used without any training on our data.

Every method gets the same load history and the same temperature forecast, and no model can see past the cutoff. The baseline, the ten percent bar and the wording of each verdict were frozen before any scored run.

Here is the receipt. A study published this week found that in Great Britain, Chronos-2 roughly ties a regression: a ratio of 0.97. Against our first baseline we measured 0.73 on Dominion, a clear win. But that baseline was weak. Against the field's standard benchmark, the ratio is 0.95: close to a tie again.

So we ran a fresh test, on two zones no model had been run on, with everything fixed in advance. Chronos-2 against the standard benchmark: 1.01 on AEP, and 0.89 on Atlantic City Electric. Neither clears our ten percent bar. No clear lead.

The leaderboard shows every model against the same baseline, two zones side by side. Each row says how many test weeks start after the model's weights were published. The grey diamonds, Timestral and TimesFM 3.0, were published after most of our test weeks, so their scores are not out of sample.
Weather matters more than the model. With better weather forecasts the regressions catch up, and against the standard benchmark Chronos-2 is level under every weather source.

Each week, two scans look for new forecasting claims: one uses Claude's built-in search, the other uses You.com. Combined, they found sixty claims, thirty-seven of them found by both. The judge agent then checks each claim against its primary sources, with every statement cited.

Here are the two scans side by side. With You.com, every search result carries a date, and a search can be limited to one site and an exact date range. So the agent ran one narrow search per site. It kept fifty-three claims against forty-four, sixteen of which Claude's search missed. And on the six claims judged both ways, the verdicts were the same.

Set up the benchmark once. Then every week: read the listings, scan, judge, run, and write the receipt. A background run never starts a model by itself. Receipts, not hype. The voice in this video is A.I. generated.
